opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a really interesting comparison, and I think it gets at why robotics has been lagging behind what we've seen with large language models.

Language, for all its richness, is fundamentally built from discrete pieces. You have a vocabulary of maybe tens of thousands of tokens, and a sentence is a sequence of those tokens. That's a huge space, but it's a structured, finite set of building blocks at each step. And critically, we have an enormous amount of it written down. The internet gave us this vast corpus of text that models could learn from.

Robot motion is different in kind. It's continuous. If you think about a robot arm with seven joints, each joint can be at any angle, moving at any velocity, applying any torque, and that's changing many times per second. So the space of possible motions is not just large, it's effectively infinite-dimensional when you consider trajectories over time. And then on top of that, you're interacting with the physical world, which brings in friction, contact, deformable objects, and tiny variations in mass and surface properties that we can't perceive directly. Two situations that look identical to a camera can behave completely differently when you actually touch them.

So you have a much harder space, and at the same time you have far less data. There's no internet of robot motions. People have estimated that the text used to train the large language models would take something like a hundred thousand years for a human to read. We're nowhere near having that equivalent for robots, and collecting it is slow and expensive because it happens in real time in the physical world.

That's why I'm a bit skeptical of the idea that we'll just scale up data and get a ChatGPT moment for robotics in the next couple of years. I think we'll get there eventually, but I suspect it will require combining learning with good old-fashioned engineering: physics, models, analytic methods. That combination is what's going to close the gap.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is something I think about a lot, because people see what large language models have done and they assume the same thing is about to happen with robots — that we'll just scale up the data and robots will suddenly be able to do everything. And I don't think that follows, and part of the reason is the nature of the space you're working in.

Language, for all its richness, is a discrete, finite thing. There's a vocabulary of, say, fifty thousand words, or a few hundred thousand tokens, and a sentence is a sequence of those. The number of sensible sentences is enormous, but it's a combinatorial structure built from a finite alphabet, and crucially, humans have been writing it down for a very long time. The internet is essentially a gigantic, free, labeled dataset of language. That's what made the whole thing possible.

Motion is different. If you think about just a robot arm with six or seven joints, the configuration of that arm is a point in a continuous space — six or seven real numbers. A motion is a continuous trajectory through that space. And it's not just the arm: you've got the object you're trying to pick up, its position and orientation, the friction between the gripper and the object, the lighting, whether the thing is deformable, whether there's a cable in the way. Every one of those is another continuous dimension, and the dynamics are coupled — if you push slightly too hard, the object rotates and everything downstream changes. So the space is uncountably infinite in a way that language just isn't, and it's full of these very sensitive, nonlinear interactions. A sentence that's off by one word is usually still a fine sentence. A grasp that's off by three millimeters drops the cup.

And the other asymmetry, which I think is underappreciated, is that we don't have the data. Nobody has been recording robot motions and their outcomes for thirty years and posting them online. Humans don't even have access to their own motor data — you can't introspect on exactly what your fingers are doing when you tie your shoes. So the equivalent of the internet for motion doesn't exist. People are trying to build it, with teleoperation and simulation and so on, and I think that's worthwhile. But when you compare the complexity of the space with the size of the dataset, the ratio is wildly worse for robotics than it ever was for language.

I'd add one caveat, which is that this is partly why language models are actually useful to robotics — not for the motion itself, but for the high-level part. "Go to the kitchen, find a mug, bring it back" — that's language, and models are good at decomposing that. Where they fall down is the last ten centimeters, the part where the hand actually has to make contact with the world. That's where the complexity lives, and I think that's going to take longer than a lot of people expect.

astra-6.text:
Well, language is enormously complex, but it’s built out of discrete elements. You have a vocabulary, and you put words together in different sequences. With robot motion, even something as simple as moving your hand involves a continuous space of possibilities. Your hand can be at different positions and orientations, and then you have all the different configurations of your arm that can put it there.

And that’s just a pose. A motion is a whole trajectory through that space. You have to decide how fast to move, whether you’ll hit something, and what happens when you make contact. If you’re picking up a glass, a small difference in where your fingers land or how much force you apply can change the outcome.

So I’d be cautious about saying one is simply more complex than the other. But the structure is very different. In robotics, we have to find motions that work in a continuous physical world, with uncertainty in both what we perceive and what we do. That’s a big part of what makes it hard.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, language is enormously rich, but it’s made up of discrete symbols. With a robot, even describing a single motion involves continuous variables: the positions of all the joints, their velocities, and how those change over time. And then there’s contact with the world, where a tiny change in position can make a big difference to what happens.

Take picking up a glass. There are many ways to approach it, many places you could put your fingers, and different amounts of force you could apply. Whether any of those works depends on things you don’t know exactly: where the glass is, how slippery it is, how heavy it is.

So I’d be cautious about saying one is simply more complex than the other. But robotics has this enormous space of possible actions, and you have to find an action that succeeds physically, under uncertainty. Producing a plausible description of picking up a glass and actually picking it up are very different achievements.
